+\begin{lemma}[Normalized saturation of rational coboundaries]
+\label{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}
+Let \(H,Q\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=Q(0)=1\).  If, for some
+integer \(m\ge1\),
+\[
+ H^m=\delta Q=\frac{Q(z^2)}{Q(z)^2},
+\]
+then there is an \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), with \(R(0)=1\), such that
+\(H=\delta R\).
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+For \(a\in\overline{\QQ}^\times\), let \(h(a)\) and \(q(a)\) denote the
+coefficients of \([a]\) in the divisors of \(H\) and \(Q\), respectively.
+Taking divisors gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:saturation-divisor-recurrence}
+ mh(a)=q(a^2)-2q(a),
+ \qquad q(a^2)\equiv2q(a)\pmod m.
+\end{equation}
+Fix \(a\ne0,\infty\).  For sufficiently large \(N\), among the
+\(2^N\)-th roots of \(a\) choose \(b_N\) outside the finite support of
+\(\operatorname{div}Q\).  Iterating the congruence along the chain from
+\(b_N\) to \(a\) gives \(q(a)\equiv2^Nq(b_N)\equiv0\pmod m\).
+The coefficient at zero is zero because \(Q(0)=1\), and the degree-zero
+condition on a principal divisor gives the same divisibility at infinity.
+Thus \(\operatorname{div}Q=mD\).
+
+The divisor \(D\) is Galois invariant and has degree zero.  Since
+\(\operatorname{Pic}^0(\mathbb P^1_{\QQ})=0\), choose
+\(S\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(\operatorname{div}S=D\), normalized by
+\(S(0)=1\).  Then \(Q/S^m\) is constant, and evaluation at zero gives
+\(Q=S^m\).  It follows that \((H/\delta S)^m=1\).  This rational function is
+constant and has value one at zero, so \(H=\delta S\); take \(R=S\).
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{proposition}[Algebraic critical products are rational coboundaries]
+\label{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}
+Let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\), \(H(0)=1\), and suppose that
+\(F\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) is algebraic over \(\CC(z)\) and satisfies
+\(F(z)^2=H(z)F(z^2)\).  Then \(H=\delta R\) for a unique
+\(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(R(0)=1\).
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(G=zF'/F\).  Logarithmic differentiation gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:log-derivative-mahler}
+ G(z)=G(z^2)+\frac z2\frac{H'(z)}{H(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+If the rational inhomogeneous term is non-zero, the equations at \(z\) and
+\(z^2\) eliminate it to give a homogeneous scalar (2)-Mahler equation for
+\(G\); if it is zero, \eqref{eq:log-derivative-mahler} and \(G(0)=0\) give
+\(G=0\).  Since algebraic functions are D-finite, B\'ezivin's theorem that a
+D-finite Mahler function is rational
+\cite[Theorem~1]{BellCoonsRowland2013MahlerDichotomy} yields
+\(G\in\CC(z)\), and its rational Taylor coefficients give
+\(G\in\QQ(z)\).
+
+All analytic branches of the algebraic function \(F\) have the same rational
+logarithmic derivative, so their pairwise quotients are constants.  Finite
+monodromy therefore gives an \(m\ge1\) for which
+\(T=F^m\) is single-valued, hence \(T\in\CC(z)^\times\).  Its Taylor
+coefficients give \(T\in\QQ(z)^\times\), and \(T(0)=1\).  Raising the
+functional equation to the (m)-th power gives
+\[
+ H^m=\frac{T(z)^2}{T(z^2)}=\delta(T^{-1}).
+\]
+Apply \Cref{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}, and then use the normalized
+injectivity proved in \Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} for uniqueness.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{theorem}[Strict-gap determinant boundary lifting]
+\label{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting}
+Let \(A\) be a primitive non-negative integer matrix with Perron root
+\(\lambda>1\), and put \(x=\lambda^{-1}\).  Let \(B,B'\) be integer matrices
+of the same size such that, entrywise,
+\[
+ \abs{B_{ij}},\abs{B'_{ij}}\le A_{ij},
+ \qquad B_{ij}\equiv B'_{ij}\equiv A_{ij}\pmod2,
+\]
+and suppose that \(\rad(B),\rad(B')<\lambda\).  Set
+\[
+ H(z)=\frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}.
+\]
+Then the following are equivalent:
+\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
+ \item \(\Pi_x(H)=1\);
+ \item there is a unique \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) such that
+ \[
+  R(0)=R(x)=1,
+  \qquad H(z)=\frac{R(z^2)}{R(z)^2}.
+ \]
+\end{enumerate}
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The strict gaps imply that both determinant polynomials are non-zero on a disk
+\(\abs z<r\) for some \(x<r<1\).  They are positive on \([0,x]\), because
+they are real, non-zero there, and equal one at zero.  Hence (H>0) on that
+interval.  Define (F) by \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-product}.  By
+\Cref{lem:critical-mahler-integrality}, it is analytic on \(\abs z<r\), has
+integer coefficients, and satisfies \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-equation}.
+Crucially, the product normalization is
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
+ F(x)^2=\Pi_x(H),
+\end{equation}
+not (F(x)=\Pi_x(H)).
+
+We apply Nishioka's special-value theorem
+\cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues} to the reduced form
+of
+\[
+ P_0(z)F(z^2)-P_1(z)F(z)^2=0.
+\]
+In her notation one may take (p=2), (N=0), (n=1), (m=2),
+(M=2), (U=1), and coefficient-growth exponent (L=1).  The required
+numerical inequality is (M(p+N)n^2=4<2^{2+1/L}=8).  The integer
+coefficients and analyticity of (F) give the required linear coefficient
+height bound, while the strict gaps ensure that the reduced coefficient
+polynomials do not vanish anywhere on the orbit (x,x^2,x^4,\ldots).
+Consequently, if (F) were transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then (F(x))
+would be transcendental.
+
+Assume (i).  Positivity and \eqref{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
+give (F(x)=1), so the cited theorem forces (F) to be algebraic.  By
+\Cref{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}, (H=\delta R) for the unique
+normalized rational (R).  Now
+\Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} gives
+(1=\Pi_x(H)=R(x)^{-2}) and (R(x)>0), hence (R(x)=1).  This proves (ii).
+Conversely, (ii) and \eqref{eq:rational-mahler-telescope} give (i), and the
+same proposition gives uniqueness.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{remark}[Scope of the lifting theorem]
+The determinant parity in \Cref{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting} is essential
+to the integrality step, so the theorem does not assert the converse for an
+arbitrary positive rational (H).  Its realizable class is nevertheless broad.
+Fix (r\ge2), an odd (a>0), and a positive even (b), and let (A) have
+diagonal entries (a) and off-diagonal entries (b).  Then
+\(\lambda=a+(r-1)b\).  Any diagonal (B=\operatorname{diag}(c_i)) and
+(B'=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)), with odd
+\(\abs{c_i},\abs{d_i}\le a\), satisfies the same-base compatibility and
+strict gaps, and realizes
+\[
+ H(z)=\frac{\prod_i(1-c_i z)}{\prod_i(1-d_i z)}.
+\]
 \end{remark}
 
 This mechanism is strictly weaker than full \(G\)-cospectrality, equivalently

+def critical_mahler_normalization_matches() -> bool:
+    """Verify that the weighted product is F(x)^2, rather than F(x)."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    x = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+    h = (1 - z) / (1 + z)
+    f = 1 - z
+    symbolic = all(
+        (
+            sp.cancel(f**2 - h * f.subs(z, z**2)) == 0,
+            f.subs(z, x) == sp.Rational(2, 3),
+            f.subs(z, x) ** 2 == sp.Rational(4, 9),
+            f.subs(z, x) != f.subs(z, x) ** 2,
+        )
+    )
+    if not symbolic:
+        return False
+
+    with mp.workdps(80):
+        real_x = mp.mpf(1) / 3
+        logarithmic_product = mp.fsum(
+            mp.power(2, -nu)
+            * mp.log((1 - real_x ** (2**nu)) / (1 + real_x ** (2**nu)))
+            for nu in range(12)
+        )
+        product_value = mp.exp(logarithmic_product)
+        return (
+            abs(product_value - mp.mpf(4) / 9) < mp.mpf("1e-70")
+            and abs(product_value - (1 - real_x)) > mp.mpf("1e-2")
+        )
+
+
+def _critical_mahler_coefficients(order: int) -> tuple[sp.Integer, ...]:
+    """Solve F^2=((1-z)/(1-3z))F(z^2) coefficient by coefficient."""
+    h_coefficients = [sp.Integer(1)] + [
+        2 * sp.Integer(3) ** (degree - 1) for degree in range(1, order + 1)
+    ]
+    coefficients = [sp.Integer(1)]
+    for degree in range(1, order + 1):
+        known_square = sum(
+            coefficients[index] * coefficients[degree - index]
+            for index in range(1, degree)
+        )
+        right_hand_side = sum(
+            h_coefficients[degree - 2 * index] * coefficients[index]
+            for index in range(degree // 2 + 1)
+        )
+        coefficients.append(sp.simplify((right_hand_side - known_square) / 2))
+    return tuple(coefficients)
+
+
+def critical_mahler_integrality_matches(order: int = 24) -> bool:
+    """Check determinant parity, integral recursion, and the truncated equation."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    p_zero = 1 - z
+    p_one = 1 - 3 * z
+    coefficients = _critical_mahler_coefficients(order)
+    f = sum(coefficient * z**degree for degree, coefficient in enumerate(coefficients))
+    residual = sp.series(
+        f**2 - (p_zero / p_one) * f.subs(z, z**2), z, 0, order + 1
+    ).removeO()
+    return all(
+        (
+            sp.Poly(p_zero - p_one, z).all_coeffs()[-1] % 2 == 0,
+            all(coefficient.is_Integer for coefficient in coefficients),
+            sp.expand(residual) == 0,
+        )
+    )
+
+
+def critical_zero_estimate_pullback_matches() -> bool:
+    """Check the cleared pullback identity and its two bidegree bounds."""
+    z, y = sp.symbols("z y")
+    p_zero = 1 - z
+    p_one = 1 - 3 * z
+    q = y**2 + z * y + z + 1
+    d = sp.Poly(q, z, y).degree(z)
+    n = sp.Poly(q, z, y).degree(y)
+    eta = max(sp.degree(p_zero, z), sp.degree(p_one, z))
+    pullback = sp.cancel(
+        p_zero**n * q.subs({z: z**2, y: p_one * y**2 / p_zero}, simultaneous=True)
+    )
+    pullback = sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).as_expr()
+    coefficients = _critical_mahler_coefficients(18)
+    f = sum(coefficient * z**degree for degree, coefficient in enumerate(coefficients))
+    evaluated_pullback = sp.series(pullback.subs(y, f), z, 0, 19).removeO()
+    expected = sp.series(
+        p_zero**n * q.subs({z: z**2, y: f.subs(z, z**2)}, simultaneous=True),
+        z,
+        0,
+        19,
+    ).removeO()
+    return all(
+        (
+            sp.Poly(q, z, y).is_irreducible,
+            sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).degree(y) <= 2 * n,
+            sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).degree(z) <= 2 * d + eta * n,
+            sp.expand(evaluated_pullback - expected) == 0,
+        )
+    )
+
+
+def rational_mahler_saturation_matches() -> bool:
+    """Verify normalized saturation identities in exact rational examples."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    examples = (
+        ((1 - z) ** 2 * (1 + 2 * z) / ((1 - 3 * z) * (1 + z) ** 3), 2),
+        ((1 + z + z**2) / ((1 - 2 * z) ** 2 * (1 + 3 * z)), 3),
+        ((1 - 4 * z) * (1 + z) ** 2 / (1 + 2 * z**2), 5),
+    )
+    for rational_r, exponent in examples:
+        rational_r = sp.cancel(rational_r)
+        h = sp.cancel(rational_r.subs(z, z**2) / rational_r**2)
+        q = sp.cancel(rational_r**exponent)
+        delta_q = sp.cancel(q.subs(z, z**2) / q**2)
+        numerator, denominator = sp.fraction(q)
+        factor_exponents = [
+            multiplicity
+            for polynomial in (numerator, denominator)
+            for _factor, multiplicity in sp.factor_list(polynomial)[1]
+        ]
+        if not all(
+            (
+                rational_r.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                h.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                q.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                sp.cancel(h**exponent - delta_q) == 0,
+                all(multiplicity % exponent == 0 for multiplicity in factor_exponents),
+            )
+        ):
+            return False
+    return True
+

+\begin{lemma}[Critical quadratic zero estimate]
+\label{lem:critical-mahler-zero-estimate}
+Let \(P_0,P_1\in\CC[z]\) have constant term one, set
+\(\eta=\max\{\deg P_0,\deg P_1\}\), and let an analytic germ
+\(F(0)=1\) satisfy
+\[
+ P_1(z)F(z)^2=P_0(z)F(z^2).
+\]
+If \(F\) is transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then every non-zero
+\(Q\in\CC[z,Y]\) with \(\deg_zQ\le D\) and \(\deg_YQ\le N\) satisfies
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-mahler-zero-bound}
+ \operatorname{ord}_{z=0}Q(z,F(z))
+ \le D+4DN+\eta N^2.
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+First take an irreducible factor \(q\in\CC[z,Y]\) of positive
+\(Y\)-degree and write \(d=\deg_zq\), \(n=\deg_Yq\).  Clear the denominator
+in its pullback by setting
+\[
+ \widetilde q(z,Y)=P_0(z)^n
+ q\!\left(z^2,\frac{P_1(z)}{P_0(z)}Y^2\right).
+\]
+This is a polynomial, with
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-pullback-orders}
+ \deg_Y\widetilde q=2n,qquad
+ \deg_z\widetilde q\le2d+\eta n,qquad
+ \operatorname{ord}_0\widetilde q(z,F(z))
+ =2\operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z)).
+\end{equation}
+We claim that \(q\nmid\widetilde q\).  Otherwise the irreducible curve
+\(C:q=0\) is invariant under the rational map
+\[
+ \Phi(z,Y)=\left(z^2,\frac{P_1(z)}{P_0(z)}Y^2\right).
+\]
+Pass to the normalization of \(C\).  The induced map permutes forward the
+finite set of places above \((0,1)\), so this finite dynamical system contains
+a periodic place.  Its Puiseux germ \(Y=G(z)\), based at \((0,1)\), therefore
+satisfies for some \(\ell\ge1\) the \(\ell\)-fold iterate of the same equation
+as \(F\).  Consequently \(U=G/F\) obeys
+\[
+ U(z^{2^\ell})=U(z)^{2^\ell},\qquad U(0)=1.
+\]
+If \(U=1+cz^\alpha+\cdots\), with \(c\ne0\) and the least positive Puiseux
+exponent \(\alpha\), the least non-constant exponents on the two sides are
+respectively \(2^\ell\alpha\) and \(\alpha\), a contradiction.  Thus
+\(U=1\), which would make \(F=G\) algebraic.  This proves the claim.
+
+Hence \(R_q(z)=\operatorname{Res}_Y(q,\widetilde q)\) is non-zero.  A
+B\'ezout identity in \(Y\), evaluated at \(Y=F(z)\), and
+\eqref{eq:critical-pullback-orders} imply
 \[
- \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
- =\frac{\prod_i(1-c_i z)}{\prod_i(1-d_i z)}.
+ \operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z))
+ \le\operatorname{ord}_0R_q
+ \le\deg R_q
+ \le4dn+\eta n^2.
 \]
-Thus the omitted converse already contains multiplicative-relation questions
-for weighted products built from these linear factors; it is not an artifact
-of dropping the same-base compatibility or strict-gap hypotheses.
+Finally write \(Q=a(z)\prod_iq_i^{e_i}\), separating its polynomial content
+in \(z\).  The content contributes at most \(D\).  With multiplicities,
+\(\sum_i e_id_i\le D\) and \(\sum_i e_in_i\le N\); therefore
+\(\sum_i e_id_in_i\le DN\) and
+\(\sum_i e_in_i^2\le N^2\).  Summing the factor bounds proves
+\eqref{eq:critical-mahler-zero-bound}.
+\end{proof}

+\begin{lemma}[Normalized saturation of rational coboundaries]
+\label{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}
+Let \(H,Q\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=Q(0)=1\).  If, for some
+integer \(m\ge1\),
+\[
+ H^m=\delta Q=\frac{Q(z^2)}{Q(z)^2},
+\]
+then there is an \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), with \(R(0)=1\), such that
+\(H=\delta R\).
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+For \(a\in\overline{\QQ}^\times\), let \(h(a)\) and \(q(a)\) denote the
+coefficients of \([a]\) in the divisors of \(H\) and \(Q\), respectively.
+Taking divisors gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:saturation-divisor-recurrence}
+ mh(a)=q(a^2)-2q(a),
+ \qquad q(a^2)\equiv2q(a)\pmod m.
+\end{equation}
+Fix \(a\ne0,\infty\).  For sufficiently large \(N\), among the
+\(2^N\)-th roots of \(a\) choose \(b_N\) outside the finite support of
+\(\operatorname{div}Q\).  Iterating the congruence along the chain from
+\(b_N\) to \(a\) gives \(q(a)\equiv2^Nq(b_N)\equiv0\pmod m\).
+The coefficient at zero is zero because \(Q(0)=1\), and the degree-zero
+condition on a principal divisor gives the same divisibility at infinity.
+Thus \(\operatorname{div}Q=mD\).
+
+The divisor \(D\) is Galois invariant and has degree zero.  Since
+\(\operatorname{Pic}^0(\mathbb P^1_{\QQ})=0\), choose
+\(S\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(\operatorname{div}S=D\), normalized by
+\(S(0)=1\).  Then \(Q/S^m\) is constant, and evaluation at zero gives
+\(Q=S^m\).  It follows that \((H/\delta S)^m=1\).  This rational function is
+constant and has value one at zero, so \(H=\delta S\); take \(R=S\).
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{proposition}[Algebraic critical products are rational coboundaries]
+\label{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}
+Let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\), \(H(0)=1\), and suppose that
+\(F\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) is algebraic over \(\CC(z)\) and satisfies
+\(F(z)^2=H(z)F(z^2)\).  Then \(H=\delta R\) for a unique
+\(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(R(0)=1\).
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(G=zF'/F\).  Logarithmic differentiation gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:log-derivative-mahler}
+ G(z)=G(z^2)+\frac z2\frac{H'(z)}{H(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+If the rational inhomogeneous term is non-zero, the equations at \(z\) and
+\(z^2\) eliminate it to give a homogeneous scalar (2)-Mahler equation for
+\(G\); if it is zero, \eqref{eq:log-derivative-mahler} and \(G(0)=0\) give
+\(G=0\).  Since algebraic functions are D-finite, B\'ezivin's theorem that a
+D-finite Mahler function is rational
+\cite[Theorem~1]{BellCoonsRowland2013MahlerDichotomy} yields
+\(G\in\CC(z)\), and its rational Taylor coefficients give
+\(G\in\QQ(z)\).
+
+All analytic branches of the algebraic function \(F\) have the same rational
+logarithmic derivative, so their pairwise quotients are constants.  Finite
+monodromy therefore gives an \(m\ge1\) for which
+\(T=F^m\) is single-valued, hence \(T\in\CC(z)^\times\).  Its Taylor
+coefficients give \(T\in\QQ(z)^\times\), and \(T(0)=1\).  Raising the
+functional equation to the (m)-th power gives
+\[
+ H^m=\frac{T(z)^2}{T(z^2)}=\delta(T^{-1}).
+\]
+Apply \Cref{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}, and then use the normalized
+injectivity proved in \Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} for uniqueness.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{theorem}[Strict-gap determinant boundary lifting]
+\label{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting}
+Let \(A\) be a primitive non-negative integer matrix with Perron root
+\(\lambda>1\), and put \(x=\lambda^{-1}\).  Let \(B,B'\) be integer matrices
+of the same size such that, entrywise,
+\[
+ \abs{B_{ij}},\abs{B'_{ij}}\le A_{ij},
+ \qquad B_{ij}\equiv B'_{ij}\equiv A_{ij}\pmod2,
+\]
+and suppose that \(\rad(B),\rad(B')<\lambda\).  Set
+\[
+ H(z)=\frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}.
+\]
+Then the following are equivalent:
+\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
+ \item \(\Pi_x(H)=1\);
+ \item there is a unique \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) such that
+ \[
+  R(0)=R(x)=1,
+  \qquad H(z)=\frac{R(z^2)}{R(z)^2}.
+ \]
+\end{enumerate}
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The strict gaps imply that both determinant polynomials are non-zero on a disk
+\(\abs z<r\) for some \(x<r<1\).  They are positive on \([0,x]\), because
+they are real, non-zero there, and equal one at zero.  Hence (H>0) on that
+interval.  Define (F) by \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-product}.  By
+\Cref{lem:critical-mahler-integrality}, it is analytic on \(\abs z<r\), has
+integer coefficients, and satisfies \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-equation}.
+Crucially, the product normalization is
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
+ F(x)^2=\Pi_x(H),
+\end{equation}
+not (F(x)=\Pi_x(H)).
+
+We apply Nishioka's special-value theorem
+\cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues} to the reduced form
+of
+\[
+ P_0(z)F(z^2)-P_1(z)F(z)^2=0.
+\]
+In her notation one may take (p=2), (N=0), (n=1), (m=2),
+(M=2), (U=1), and coefficient-growth exponent (L=1).  The required
+numerical inequality is (M(p+N)n^2=4<2^{2+1/L}=8).  The integer
+coefficients and analyticity of (F) give the required linear coefficient
+height bound, while the strict gaps ensure that the reduced coefficient
+polynomials do not vanish anywhere on the orbit (x,x^2,x^4,\ldots).
+Consequently, if (F) were transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then (F(x))
+would be transcendental.
+
+Assume (i).  Positivity and \eqref{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
+give (F(x)=1), so the cited theorem forces (F) to be algebraic.  By
+\Cref{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}, (H=\delta R) for the unique
+normalized rational (R).  Now
+\Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} gives
+(1=\Pi_x(H)=R(x)^{-2}) and (R(x)>0), hence (R(x)=1).  This proves (ii).
+Conversely, (ii) and \eqref{eq:rational-mahler-telescope} give (i), and the
+same proposition gives uniqueness.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{remark}[Scope of the lifting theorem]
+The determinant parity in \Cref{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting} is essential
+to the integrality step, so the theorem does not assert the converse for an
+arbitrary positive rational (H).  Its realizable class is nevertheless broad.
+Fix (r\ge2), an odd (a>0), and a positive even (b), and let (A) have
+diagonal entries (a) and off-diagonal entries (b).  Then
+\(\lambda=a+(r-1)b\).  Any diagonal (B=\operatorname{diag}(c_i)) and
+(B'=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)), with odd
+\(\abs{c_i},\abs{d_i}\le a\), satisfies the same-base compatibility and
+strict gaps, and realizes
+\[
+ H(z)=\frac{\prod_i(1-c_i z)}{\prod_i(1-d_i z)}.
+\]
 \end{remark}
 
 This mechanism is strictly weaker than full \(G\)-cospectrality, equivalently

 243: We now prove that the converse in
 244: \eqref{eq:positive-rational-certificate-kernel} does hold for strict-gap
 245: determinant ratios arising from two sign blocks on one base.  The argument has
 246: two arithmetic inputs.  The first is the Dieudonn\'e--Dwork integrality
 247: criterion; the second is Nishioka's published special-value theorem for
 248: implicit Mahler equations.  We isolate the parts specific to the present
 249: determinant setting.
 250: 
 251: \begin{lemma}[Integral critical Mahler product]
 252: \label{lem:critical-mahler-integrality}
 253: Let \(B,B'\) be integer matrices such that \(B\equiv B'\pmod 2\), put
 254: \[
 255:  P_0(z)=\det(I-zB),\qquad P_1(z)=\det(I-zB'),\qquad
 256:  H(z)=\frac{P_0(z)}{P_1(z)},
 257: \]
 258: and suppose that both determinant polynomials are zero-free on \(\abs z<r\),
 259: where \(0<r\le1\).  On this disk define
 260: \begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-mahler-product}
 261:  F(z)=\prod_{\nu\ge0}H(z^{2^\nu})^{2^{-\nu-1}},
 262:  \qquad F(0)=1,
 263: \end{equation}
 264: using the logarithm germ at zero.  Then \(F\) is analytic and non-vanishing,
 265: \begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-mahler-equation}
 266:  F(z)^2=H(z)F(z^2),
 267: \end{equation}
 268: and \(F\in\ZZ[[z]]\).
 269: \end{lemma}
 270: 
 271: \begin{proof}
 272: Normal convergence of the logarithmic series on compact subdisks proves the
 273: analytic assertions and shifting the product proves
 274: \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-equation}.  The determinant congruence gives
 275: \(P_0\equiv P_1\pmod2\), hence
 276: \[
 277:  H(z)^{-1}\in1+2z\ZZ_2[[z]].
 278: \]
 279: Since
 280: \(F(z^2)/F(z)^2=H(z)^{-1}\), the Dieudonn\'e--Dwork criterion
 281: \cite[Theorem~1.1]{PomeratStraub2024RootsPowerSeries} gives
 282: \(F\in\ZZ_2[[z]]\).  Also \(F\in\QQ[[z]]\), directly from
 283: \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-product}.  For an odd prime \(p\), compare the
 284: coefficient of \(z^n\) in \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-equation}.  Its left-hand
 285: side is \(2f_n\) plus an expression in \(f_0,\ldots,f_{n-1}\), while its
 286: right-hand side belongs to \(\ZZ_p\) whenever the preceding coefficients do,
 287: because \(P_1(0)=1\).  Induction and \(2\in\ZZ_p^\times\) give
 288: \(F\in\ZZ_p[[z]]\) for every odd \(p\).  A rational number integral at every
 289: prime is an integer, proving the claim coefficientwise.
 290: \end{proof}
 291: 
 292: The next estimate is not needed to reprove the special-value theorem below;
 293: it records an effective feature of the critical quadratic equation itself.
 294: 
 295: \begin{lemma}[Critical quadratic zero estimate]
 296: \label{lem:critical-mahler-zero-estimate}
 297: Let \(P_0,P_1\in\CC[z]\) have constant term one, set
 298: \(\eta=\max\{\deg P_0,\deg P_1\}\), and let an analytic germ
 299: \(F(0)=1\) satisfy
 300: \[
 301:  P_1(z)F(z)^2=P_0(z)F(z^2).
 302: \]
 303: If \(F\) is transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then every non-zero
 304: \(Q\in\CC[z,Y]\) with \(\deg_zQ\le D\) and \(\deg_YQ\le N\) satisfies
 305: \begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-mahler-zero-bound}
 306:  \operatorname{ord}_{z=0}Q(z,F(z))
 307:  \le D+4DN+\eta N^2.
 308: \end{equation}
 309: \end{lemma}
 310: 
 311: \begin{proof}
 312: First take an irreducible factor \(q\in\CC[z,Y]\) of positive
 313: \(Y\)-degree and write \(d=\deg_zq\), \(n=\deg_Yq\).  Clear the denominator
 314: in its pullback by setting
 315: \[
 316:  \widetilde q(z,Y)=P_0(z)^n
 317:  q\!\left(z^2,\frac{P_1(z)}{P_0(z)}Y^2\right).
 318: \]
 319: This is a polynomial, with
 320: \begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-pullback-orders}
 321:  \deg_Y\widetilde q=2n,qquad
 322:  \deg_z\widetilde q\le2d+\eta n,qquad
 323:  \operatorname{ord}_0\widetilde q(z,F(z))
 324:  =2\operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z)).
 325: \end{equation}
 326: We claim that \(q\nmid\widetilde q\).  Otherwise the irreducible curve
 327: \(C:q=0\) is invariant under the rational map
 328: \[
 329:  \Phi(z,Y)=\left(z^2,\frac{P_1(z)}{P_0(z)}Y^2\right).
 330: \]
 331: Pass to the normalization of \(C\).  The induced map permutes forward the
 332: finite set of places above \((0,1)\), so this finite dynamical system contains
 333: a periodic place.  Its Puiseux germ \(Y=G(z)\), based at \((0,1)\), therefore
 334: satisfies for some \(\ell\ge1\) the \(\ell\)-fold iterate of the same equation
 335: as \(F\).  Consequently \(U=G/F\) obeys
 336: \[
 337:  U(z^{2^\ell})=U(z)^{2^\ell},\qquad U(0)=1.
 338: \]
 339: If \(U=1+cz^\alpha+\cdots\), with \(c\ne0\) and the least positive Puiseux
 340: exponent \(\alpha\), the least non-constant exponents on the two sides are
 341: respectively \(2^\ell\alpha\) and \(\alpha\), a contradiction.  Thus
 342: \(U=1\), which would make \(F=G\) algebraic.  This proves the claim.
 343: 
 344: Hence \(R_q(z)=\operatorname{Res}_Y(q,\widetilde q)\) is non-zero.  A
 345: B\'ezout identity in \(Y\), evaluated at \(Y=F(z)\), and
 346: \eqref{eq:critical-pullback-orders} imply
 347: \[
 348:  \operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z))
 349:  \le\operatorname{ord}_0R_q
 350:  \le\deg R_q
 351:  \le4dn+\eta n^2.
 352: \]
 353: Finally write \(Q=a(z)\prod_iq_i^{e_i}\), separating its polynomial content
 354: in \(z\).  The content contributes at most \(D\).  With multiplicities,
 355: \(\sum_i e_id_i\le D\) and \(\sum_i e_in_i\le N\); therefore
 356: \(\sum_i e_id_in_i\le DN\) and
 357: \(\sum_i e_in_i^2\le N^2\).  Summing the factor bounds proves
 358: \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-zero-bound}.
 359: \end{proof}
 360: 
 361: \begin{lemma}[Normalized saturation of rational coboundaries]
 362: \label{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}
 363: Let \(H,Q\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=Q(0)=1\).  If, for some
 364: integer \(m\ge1\),
 365: \[
 366:  H^m=\delta Q=\frac{Q(z^2)}{Q(z)^2},
 367: \]
 368: then there is an \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), with \(R(0)=1\), such that
 369: \(H=\delta R\).
 370: \end{lemma}
 371: 
 372: \begin{proof}
 373: For \(a\in\overline{\QQ}^\times\), let \(h(a)\) and \(q(a)\) denote the
 374: coefficients of \([a]\) in the divisors of \(H\) and \(Q\), respectively.
 375: Taking divisors gives
 376: \begin{equation}\label{eq:saturation-divisor-recurrence}
 377:  mh(a)=q(a^2)-2q(a),
 378:  \qquad q(a^2)\equiv2q(a)\pmod m.
 379: \end{equation}
 380: Fix \(a\ne0,\infty\).  For sufficiently large \(N\), among the
 381: \(2^N\)-th roots of \(a\) choose \(b_N\) outside the finite support of
 382: \(\operatorname{div}Q\).  Iterating the congruence along the chain from
 383: \(b_N\) to \(a\) gives \(q(a)\equiv2^Nq(b_N)\equiv0\pmod m\).
 384: The coefficient at zero is zero because \(Q(0)=1\), and the degree-zero
 385: condition on a principal divisor gives the same divisibility at infinity.
 386: Thus \(\operatorname{div}Q=mD\).
 387: 
 388: The divisor \(D\) is Galois invariant and has degree zero.  Since
 389: \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(\mathbb P^1_{\QQ})=0\), choose
 390: \(S\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(\operatorname{div}S=D\), normalized by
 391: \(S(0)=1\).  Then \(Q/S^m\) is constant, and evaluation at zero gives
 392: \(Q=S^m\).  It follows that \((H/\delta S)^m=1\).  This rational function is
 393: constant and has value one at zero, so \(H=\delta S\); take \(R=S\).
 394: \end{proof}
 395: 
 396: \begin{proposition}[Algebraic critical products are rational coboundaries]
 397: \label{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}
 398: Let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\), \(H(0)=1\), and suppose that
 399: \(F\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) is algebraic over \(\CC(z)\) and satisfies
 400: \(F(z)^2=H(z)F(z^2)\).  Then \(H=\delta R\) for a unique
 401: \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(R(0)=1\).
 402: \end{proposition}
 403: 
 404: \begin{proof}
 405: Put \(G=zF'/F\).  Logarithmic differentiation gives
 406: \begin{equation}\label{eq:log-derivative-mahler}
 407:  G(z)=G(z^2)+\frac z2\frac{H'(z)}{H(z)}.
 408: \end{equation}
 409: If the rational inhomogeneous term is non-zero, the equations at \(z\) and
 410: \(z^2\) eliminate it to give a homogeneous scalar (2)-Mahler equation for
 411: \(G\); if it is zero, \eqref{eq:log-derivative-mahler} and \(G(0)=0\) give
 412: \(G=0\).  Since algebraic functions are D-finite, B\'ezivin's theorem that a
 413: D-finite Mahler function is rational
 414: \cite[Theorem~1]{BellCoonsRowland2013MahlerDichotomy} yields
 415: \(G\in\CC(z)\), and its rational Taylor coefficients give
 416: \(G\in\QQ(z)\).
 417: 
 418: All analytic branches of the algebraic function \(F\) have the same rational
 419: logarithmic derivative, so their pairwise quotients are constants.  Finite
 420: monodromy therefore gives an \(m\ge1\) for which
 421: \(T=F^m\) is single-valued, hence \(T\in\CC(z)^\times\).  Its Taylor
 422: coefficients give \(T\in\QQ(z)^\times\), and \(T(0)=1\).  Raising the
 423: functional equation to the (m)-th power gives
 424: \[
 425:  H^m=\frac{T(z)^2}{T(z^2)}=\delta(T^{-1}).
 426: \]
 427: Apply \Cref{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}, and then use the normalized
 428: injectivity proved in \Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} for uniqueness.
 429: \end{proof}
 430: 
 431: \begin{theorem}[Strict-gap determinant boundary lifting]
 432: \label{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting}
 433: Let \(A\) be a primitive non-negative integer matrix with Perron root
 434: \(\lambda>1\), and put \(x=\lambda^{-1}\).  Let \(B,B'\) be integer matrices
 435: of the same size such that, entrywise,
 436: \[
 437:  \abs{B_{ij}},\abs{B'_{ij}}\le A_{ij},
 438:  \qquad B_{ij}\equiv B'_{ij}\equiv A_{ij}\pmod2,
 439: \]
 440: and suppose that \(\rad(B),\rad(B')<\lambda\).  Set
 441: \[
 442:  H(z)=\frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}.
 443: \]
 444: Then the following are equivalent:
 445: \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
 446:  \item \(\Pi_x(H)=1\);
 447:  \item there is a unique \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) such that
 448:  \[
 449:   R(0)=R(x)=1,
 450:   \qquad H(z)=\frac{R(z^2)}{R(z)^2}.
 451:  \]
 452: \end{enumerate}
 453: \end{theorem}
 454: 
 455: \begin{proof}
 456: The strict gaps imply that both determinant polynomials are non-zero on a disk
 457: \(\abs z<r\) for some \(x<r<1\).  They are positive on \([0,x]\), because
 458: they are real, non-zero there, and equal one at zero.  Hence (H>0) on that
 459: interval.  Define (F) by \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-product}.  By
 460: \Cref{lem:critical-mahler-integrality}, it is analytic on \(\abs z<r\), has
 461: integer coefficients, and satisfies \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-equation}.
 462: Crucially, the product normalization is
 463: \begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
 464:  F(x)^2=\Pi_x(H),
 465: \end{equation}
 466: not (F(x)=\Pi_x(H)).
 467: 
 468: We apply Nishioka's special-value theorem
 469: \cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues} to the reduced form
 470: of
 471: \[
 472:  P_0(z)F(z^2)-P_1(z)F(z)^2=0.
 473: \]
 474: In her notation one may take (p=2), (N=0), (n=1), (m=2),
 475: (M=2), (U=1), and coefficient-growth exponent (L=1).  The required
 476: numerical inequality is (M(p+N)n^2=4<2^{2+1/L}=8).  The integer
 477: coefficients and analyticity of (F) give the required linear coefficient
 478: height bound, while the strict gaps ensure that the reduced coefficient
 479: polynomials do not vanish anywhere on the orbit (x,x^2,x^4,\ldots).
 480: Consequently, if (F) were transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then (F(x))
 481: would be transcendental.
 482: 
 483: Assume (i).  Positivity and \eqref{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
 484: give (F(x)=1), so the cited theorem forces (F) to be algebraic.  By
 485: \Cref{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}, (H=\delta R) for the unique
 486: normalized rational (R).  Now
 487: \Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} gives
 488: (1=\Pi_x(H)=R(x)^{-2}) and (R(x)>0), hence (R(x)=1).  This proves (ii).
 489: Conversely, (ii) and \eqref{eq:rational-mahler-telescope} give (i), and the
 490: same proposition gives uniqueness.
 491: \end{proof}
 492: 
 493: \begin{remark}[Scope of the lifting theorem]
 494: The determinant parity in \Cref{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting} is essential
 495: to the integrality step, so the theorem does not assert the converse for an
 496: arbitrary positive rational (H).  Its realizable class is nevertheless broad.
 497: Fix (r\ge2), an odd (a>0), and a positive even (b), and let (A) have
 498: diagonal entries (a) and off-diagonal entries (b).  Then
 499: \(\lambda=a+(r-1)b\).  Any diagonal (B=\operatorname{diag}(c_i)) and
 500: (B'=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)), with odd
 501: \(\abs{c_i},\abs{d_i}\le a\), satisfies the same-base compatibility and
 502: strict gaps, and realizes
 503: \[
 504:  H(z)=\frac{\prod_i(1-c_i z)}{\prod_i(1-d_i z)}.
 505: \]
 506: \end{remark}
 507: 
 508: This mechanism is strictly weaker than full \(G\)-cospectrality, equivalently
 509: represented cospectrality in every irreducible representation:
 510: \eqref{eq:c2-collision-first-determinant} and
 511: \eqref{eq:c2-collision-second-determinant} are different.  Represented
 512: cospectrality in every irreducible representation instead requires equality
 513: of the full twisted spectra and therefore preserves the complete periodic profile
 514: \cite{BoyleSchmieding2017FiniteGroupExtensions,
 515: CavaleriDonno2022Cospectrality}.
 516: 
 517: We next delimit the finite minimality assertion.  A \emph{regular polynomial
 518: \(C_2\)-certificate} is a tuple \((A,B,B',Q)\) in which \(A\) is a primitive
 519: \(m\)-out-regular integral adjacency matrix, \(B,B'\) are compatible sign
 520: blocks, \(Q\in\ZZ[z]\) is non-constant with \(Q(0)=Q(1/m)=1\), both sign
 521: blocks have spectral radius less than \(m\), and
 522: \begin{equation}\label{eq:regular-polynomial-certificate}
 523:  \det(I-zB)=Q(z^2),
 524:  \qquad
 525:  \det(I-zB')=Q(z)^2.
 526: \end{equation}
 527: Its complexity is ordered lexicographically as
 528: \[
 529:  \bigl(2,\deg Q,|V|,m,|E|\bigr).
 530: \]
 531: 
 532: \begin{proposition}[Minimality in the regular polynomial certificate class]
 533: \label{prop:c2-certificate-minimality}
 534: The certificate in \Cref{thm:c2-boundary-collision} has complexity
 535: \((2,2,4,4,16)\), and this is the least complexity of a regular polynomial
 536: \(C_2\)-certificate.
 537: \end{proposition}
 538: 
 539: \begin{proof}
 540: The first coordinate is fixed by the non-trivial binary group.  Since
 541: \(Q(0)=Q(1/m)=1\), a non-constant \(Q\) cannot have degree one, so
 542: \(\deg Q\ge2\).  If \(\deg Q=2\), then \(Q(z^2)\) has degree four, whereas
 543: \(\deg\det(I-zB)\le |V|\); hence \(|V|\ge4\).
 544: 
 545: It remains to exclude \(m=2,3\) at \(\deg Q=2\) and \(|V|=4\).  Write
 546: \begin{equation}\label{eq:minimality-q-form}
 547:  Q(z)=1-kz+kmz^2,
 548:  \qquad k\in\ZZ\setminus\{0\},
 549: \end{equation}
 550: which follows from \(Q(1/m)=1\).  When \(m=2\), the characteristic
 551: polynomial forced by the second identity in
 552: \eqref{eq:regular-polynomial-certificate} is
 553: \((x^2-kx+2k)^2\).  If its roots have modulus strictly less than two, their
 554: product gives \(|k|<2\).  The choice \(k=-1\) has a root \(-2\), and
 555: \(k=0\) makes \(Q\) constant; therefore strict gap forces \(k=1\).
 556: 
 557: There are exactly ten non-negative integral four-entry rows of sum two,
 558: namely \(2e_i\) and \(e_i+e_j\) for \(i<j\).  We exhaust the resulting
 559: \(10^4\) matrices.  Primitivity is decided exactly by testing positivity of
 560: a power through exponent ten, the four-dimensional Wielandt bound.  This
 561: leaves \(2208\) primitive base matrices.  For each such matrix, every
 562: compatible signed entry is enumerated from
 563: \[
 564:  B_{ij}\in\{-A_{ij},-A_{ij}+2,\ldots,A_{ij}\}.
 565: \]
 566: For an integral \(4\times4\) matrix, put \(t_r=\Tr(B^r)\).  Newton's
 567: identities give
 568: \[
 569:  \det(I-zB)=1-t_1z+\frac{t_1^2-t_2}{2}z^2
 570:  -\frac{t_1^3-3t_1t_2+2t_3}{6}z^3+\det(B)z^4.
 571: \]
 572: Thus the two target polynomials
 573: \(1-z^2+2z^4\) and \((1-z+2z^2)^2\) are tested by the integer quadruples
 574: \[
 575:  (t_1,t_2,t_3,\det B)=(0,2,0,2),
 576:  \qquad (2,-6,-10,4),
 577: \]
 578: respectively.  The exhaustive integer enumeration finds \(48\) primitive
 579: bases supporting the first target and no primitive base supporting the
 580: second.  Hence no certificate exists for \(m=2\).  The enumeration and all
 581: counts are reproduced by the exact-arithmetic verifier cited in
 582: \Cref{sec:exactness}.
 583: 
 584: When \(m=3\), compatibility gives
 585: \(B\mathbf1\equiv A\mathbf1\equiv\mathbf1\pmod2\).  Therefore
 586: \(I-B\) is singular over \(\mathbb F_2\) and \(\det(I-B)\) is even.  On the
 587: other hand, the first identity in
 588: \eqref{eq:regular-polynomial-certificate} and
 589: \eqref{eq:minimality-q-form} give
 590: \[
 591:  \det(I-B)=Q(1)=1-k+3k=1+2k,
 592: \]
 593: which is odd.  Thus \(m=3\) is impossible.  Since \(m>1\), it follows that
 594: \(m\ge4\), and regularity gives \(|E|=m|V|\ge16\).  The matrices in
 595: \Cref{thm:c2-boundary-collision} attain every bound.
 596: \end{proof}
 597: 
 598: The minimality assertion is deliberately confined to the finite polynomial
 599: certificate class in \eqref{eq:regular-polynomial-certificate}; it does not
 600: purport to classify possible isolated equalities of transcendental boundary
 601: values lacking such a certificate.
 602: 
 603: Although one Perron-point value loses information, an analytic radial profile
 604: restores it.  The following is a sufficient recovery criterion; no optimality
 605: claim about the amount of profile data is intended.
 606: 
 607: \begin{theorem}[Radial-profile recovery]
 608: \label{thm:radial-profile-recovery}
 609: Let \(\tau,\tau':E(\Gamma)\to G\) be two labellings on the same primitive
 610: base matrix, both satisfying the strict twisted gap.  For every conjugacy
 611: class \(C\), define
 612: \begin{equation}\label{eq:radial-profile-difference}
 613:  D_C(z):=\sum_{n\ge1}
 614:  \bigl(p_{n,C}(\tau)-p_{n,C}(\tau')\bigr)\log(1-z^n),
 615: \end{equation}
 616: where the logarithm is normalized at zero.  There is a number
 617: \(1<\beta<\lambda\) for which every \(D_C\) is analytic on
 618: \(|z|<\beta^{-1}\).  If, for every \(C\), \(D_C\) vanishes on a set
 619: \(S\subset\{|z|<\beta^{-1}\}\) having an accumulation point in that disc,
 620: then

+def critical_mahler_normalization_matches() -> bool:
+    """Verify that the weighted product is F(x)^2, rather than F(x)."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    x = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+    h = (1 - z) / (1 + z)
+    f = 1 - z
+    symbolic = all(
+        (
+            sp.cancel(f**2 - h * f.subs(z, z**2)) == 0,
+            f.subs(z, x) == sp.Rational(2, 3),
+            f.subs(z, x) ** 2 == sp.Rational(4, 9),
+            f.subs(z, x) != f.subs(z, x) ** 2,
+        )
+    )
+    if not symbolic:
+        return False
+
+    with mp.workdps(80):
+        real_x = mp.mpf(1) / 3
+        logarithmic_product = mp.fsum(
+            mp.power(2, -nu)
+            * mp.log((1 - real_x ** (2**nu)) / (1 + real_x ** (2**nu)))
+            for nu in range(12)
+        )
+        product_value = mp.exp(logarithmic_product)
+        return (
+            abs(product_value - mp.mpf(4) / 9) < mp.mpf("1e-70")
+            and abs(product_value - (1 - real_x)) > mp.mpf("1e-2")
+        )
+
+
+def _critical_mahler_coefficients(order: int) -> tuple[sp.Integer, ...]:
+    """Solve F^2=((1-z)/(1-3z))F(z^2) coefficient by coefficient."""
+    h_coefficients = [sp.Integer(1)] + [
+        2 * sp.Integer(3) ** (degree - 1) for degree in range(1, order + 1)
+    ]
+    coefficients = [sp.Integer(1)]
+    for degree in range(1, order + 1):
+        known_square = sum(
+            coefficients[index] * coefficients[degree - index]
+            for index in range(1, degree)
+        )
+        right_hand_side = sum(
+            h_coefficients[degree - 2 * index] * coefficients[index]
+            for index in range(degree // 2 + 1)
+        )
+        coefficients.append(sp.simplify((right_hand_side - known_square) / 2))
+    return tuple(coefficients)
+
+
+def critical_mahler_integrality_matches(order: int = 24) -> bool:
+    """Check determinant parity, integral recursion, and the truncated equation."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    p_zero = 1 - z
+    p_one = 1 - 3 * z
+    coefficients = _critical_mahler_coefficients(order)
+    f = sum(coefficient * z**degree for degree, coefficient in enumerate(coefficients))
+    residual = sp.series(
+        f**2 - (p_zero / p_one) * f.subs(z, z**2), z, 0, order + 1
+    ).removeO()
+    return all(
+        (
+            sp.Poly(p_zero - p_one, z).all_coeffs()[-1] % 2 == 0,
+            all(coefficient.is_Integer for coefficient in coefficients),
+            sp.expand(residual) == 0,
+        )
+    )
+
+
+def critical_zero_estimate_pullback_matches() -> bool:
+    """Check the cleared pullback identity and its two bidegree bounds."""
+    z, y = sp.symbols("z y")
+    p_zero = 1 - z
+    p_one = 1 - 3 * z
+    q = y**2 + z * y + z + 1
+    d = sp.Poly(q, z, y).degree(z)
+    n = sp.Poly(q, z, y).degree(y)
+    eta = max(sp.degree(p_zero, z), sp.degree(p_one, z))
+    pullback = sp.cancel(
+        p_zero**n * q.subs({z: z**2, y: p_one * y**2 / p_zero}, simultaneous=True)
+    )
+    pullback = sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).as_expr()
+    coefficients = _critical_mahler_coefficients(18)
+    f = sum(coefficient * z**degree for degree, coefficient in enumerate(coefficients))
+    evaluated_pullback = sp.series(pullback.subs(y, f), z, 0, 19).removeO()
+    expected = sp.series(
+        p_zero**n * q.subs({z: z**2, y: f.subs(z, z**2)}, simultaneous=True),
+        z,
+        0,
+        19,
+    ).removeO()
+    return all(
+        (
+            sp.Poly(q, z, y).is_irreducible,
+            sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).degree(y) <= 2 * n,
+            sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).degree(z) <= 2 * d + eta * n,
+            sp.expand(evaluated_pullback - expected) == 0,
+        )
+    )
+
+
+def rational_mahler_saturation_matches() -> bool:
+    """Verify normalized saturation identities in exact rational examples."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    examples = (
+        ((1 - z) ** 2 * (1 + 2 * z) / ((1 - 3 * z) * (1 + z) ** 3), 2),
+        ((1 + z + z**2) / ((1 - 2 * z) ** 2 * (1 + 3 * z)), 3),
+        ((1 - 4 * z) * (1 + z) ** 2 / (1 + 2 * z**2), 5),
+    )
+    for rational_r, exponent in examples:
+        rational_r = sp.cancel(rational_r)
+        h = sp.cancel(rational_r.subs(z, z**2) / rational_r**2)
+        q = sp.cancel(rational_r**exponent)
+        delta_q = sp.cancel(q.subs(z, z**2) / q**2)
+        numerator, denominator = sp.fraction(q)
+        factor_exponents = [
+            multiplicity
+            for polynomial in (numerator, denominator)
+            for _factor, multiplicity in sp.factor_list(polynomial)[1]
+        ]
+        if not all(
+            (
+                rational_r.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                h.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                q.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                sp.cancel(h**exponent - delta_q) == 0,
+                all(multiplicity % exponent == 0 for multiplicity in factor_exponents),
+            )
+        ):
+            return False
+    return True
+

+\begin{lemma}[Critical quadratic zero estimate]
+\label{lem:critical-mahler-zero-estimate}
+Let \(P_0,P_1\in\CC[z]\) have constant term one, set
+\(\eta=\max\{\deg P_0,\deg P_1\}\), and let an analytic germ
+\(F(0)=1\) satisfy
+\[
+ P_1(z)F(z)^2=P_0(z)F(z^2).
+\]
+If \(F\) is transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then every non-zero
+\(Q\in\CC[z,Y]\) with \(\deg_zQ\le D\) and \(\deg_YQ\le N\) satisfies
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-mahler-zero-bound}
+ \operatorname{ord}_{z=0}Q(z,F(z))
+ \le D+4DN+\eta N^2.
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+First take an irreducible factor \(q\in\CC[z,Y]\) of positive
+\(Y\)-degree and write \(d=\deg_zq\), \(n=\deg_Yq\).  Clear the denominator
+in its pullback by setting
+\[
+ \widetilde q(z,Y)=P_0(z)^n
+ q\!\left(z^2,\frac{P_1(z)}{P_0(z)}Y^2\right).
+\]
+This is a polynomial, with
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-pullback-orders}
+ \deg_Y\widetilde q=2n,qquad
+ \deg_z\widetilde q\le2d+\eta n,qquad
+ \operatorname{ord}_0\widetilde q(z,F(z))
+ =2\operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z)).
+\end{equation}
+We claim that \(q\nmid\widetilde q\).  Otherwise the irreducible curve
+\(C:q=0\) is invariant under the rational map
+\[
+ \Phi(z,Y)=\left(z^2,\frac{P_1(z)}{P_0(z)}Y^2\right).
+\]
+Pass to the normalization of \(C\).  The induced map permutes forward the
+finite set of places above \((0,1)\), so this finite dynamical system contains
+a periodic place.  Its Puiseux germ \(Y=G(z)\), based at \((0,1)\), therefore
+satisfies for some \(\ell\ge1\) the \(\ell\)-fold iterate of the same equation
+as \(F\).  Consequently \(U=G/F\) obeys
+\[
+ U(z^{2^\ell})=U(z)^{2^\ell},\qquad U(0)=1.
+\]
+If \(U=1+cz^\alpha+\cdots\), with \(c\ne0\) and the least positive Puiseux
+exponent \(\alpha\), the least non-constant exponents on the two sides are
+respectively \(2^\ell\alpha\) and \(\alpha\), a contradiction.  Thus
+\(U=1\), which would make \(F=G\) algebraic.  This proves the claim.
+
+Hence \(R_q(z)=\operatorname{Res}_Y(q,\widetilde q)\) is non-zero.  A
+B\'ezout identity in \(Y\), evaluated at \(Y=F(z)\), and
+\eqref{eq:critical-pullback-orders} imply
 \[
- \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
- =\frac{\prod_i(1-c_i z)}{\prod_i(1-d_i z)}.
+ \operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z))
+ \le\operatorname{ord}_0R_q
+ \le\deg R_q
+ \le4dn+\eta n^2.
 \]

+\begin{lemma}[Normalized saturation of rational coboundaries]
+\label{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}
+Let \(H,Q\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=Q(0)=1\).  If, for some
+integer \(m\ge1\),
+\[
+ H^m=\delta Q=\frac{Q(z^2)}{Q(z)^2},
+\]
+then there is an \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), with \(R(0)=1\), such that
+\(H=\delta R\).
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+For \(a\in\overline{\QQ}^\times\), let \(h(a)\) and \(q(a)\) denote the
+coefficients of \([a]\) in the divisors of \(H\) and \(Q\), respectively.
+Taking divisors gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:saturation-divisor-recurrence}
+ mh(a)=q(a^2)-2q(a),
+ \qquad q(a^2)\equiv2q(a)\pmod m.
+\end{equation}
+Fix \(a\ne0,\infty\).  For sufficiently large \(N\), among the
+\(2^N\)-th roots of \(a\) choose \(b_N\) outside the finite support of
+\(\operatorname{div}Q\).  Iterating the congruence along the chain from
+\(b_N\) to \(a\) gives \(q(a)\equiv2^Nq(b_N)\equiv0\pmod m\).
+The coefficient at zero is zero because \(Q(0)=1\), and the degree-zero
+condition on a principal divisor gives the same divisibility at infinity.
+Thus \(\operatorname{div}Q=mD\).
+
+The divisor \(D\) is Galois invariant and has degree zero.  Since
+\(\operatorname{Pic}^0(\mathbb P^1_{\QQ})=0\), choose
+\(S\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(\operatorname{div}S=D\), normalized by
+\(S(0)=1\).  Then \(Q/S^m\) is constant, and evaluation at zero gives
+\(Q=S^m\).  It follows that \((H/\delta S)^m=1\).  This rational function is
+constant and has value one at zero, so \(H=\delta S\); take \(R=S\).
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{proposition}[Algebraic critical products are rational coboundaries]
+\label{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}
+Let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\), \(H(0)=1\), and suppose that
+\(F\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) is algebraic over \(\CC(z)\) and satisfies
+\(F(z)^2=H(z)F(z^2)\).  Then \(H=\delta R\) for a unique
+\(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(R(0)=1\).
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(G=zF'/F\).  Logarithmic differentiation gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:log-derivative-mahler}
+ G(z)=G(z^2)+\frac z2\frac{H'(z)}{H(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+If the rational inhomogeneous term is non-zero, the equations at \(z\) and
+\(z^2\) eliminate it to give a homogeneous scalar (2)-Mahler equation for
+\(G\); if it is zero, \eqref{eq:log-derivative-mahler} and \(G(0)=0\) give
+\(G=0\).  Since algebraic functions are D-finite, B\'ezivin's theorem that a
+D-finite Mahler function is rational
+\cite[Theorem~1]{BellCoonsRowland2013MahlerDichotomy} yields
+\(G\in\CC(z)\), and its rational Taylor coefficients give
+\(G\in\QQ(z)\).
+
+All analytic branches of the algebraic function \(F\) have the same rational
+logarithmic derivative, so their pairwise quotients are constants.  Finite
+monodromy therefore gives an \(m\ge1\) for which
+\(T=F^m\) is single-valued, hence \(T\in\CC(z)^\times\).  Its Taylor
+coefficients give \(T\in\QQ(z)^\times\), and \(T(0)=1\).  Raising the
+functional equation to the (m)-th power gives
+\[
+ H^m=\frac{T(z)^2}{T(z^2)}=\delta(T^{-1}).
+\]
+Apply \Cref{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}, and then use the normalized
+injectivity proved in \Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} for uniqueness.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{theorem}[Strict-gap determinant boundary lifting]
+\label{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting}
+Let \(A\) be a primitive non-negative integer matrix with Perron root
+\(\lambda>1\), and put \(x=\lambda^{-1}\).  Let \(B,B'\) be integer matrices
+of the same size such that, entrywise,
+\[
+ \abs{B_{ij}},\abs{B'_{ij}}\le A_{ij},
+ \qquad B_{ij}\equiv B'_{ij}\equiv A_{ij}\pmod2,
+\]
+and suppose that \(\rad(B),\rad(B')<\lambda\).  Set
+\[
+ H(z)=\frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}.
+\]
+Then the following are equivalent:
+\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
+ \item \(\Pi_x(H)=1\);
+ \item there is a unique \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) such that
+ \[
+  R(0)=R(x)=1,
+  \qquad H(z)=\frac{R(z^2)}{R(z)^2}.
+ \]
+\end{enumerate}
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The strict gaps imply that both determinant polynomials are non-zero on a disk
+\(\abs z<r\) for some \(x<r<1\).  They are positive on \([0,x]\), because
+they are real, non-zero there, and equal one at zero.  Hence (H>0) on that
+interval.  Define (F) by \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-product}.  By
+\Cref{lem:critical-mahler-integrality}, it is analytic on \(\abs z<r\), has
+integer coefficients, and satisfies \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-equation}.
+Crucially, the product normalization is
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
+ F(x)^2=\Pi_x(H),
+\end{equation}
+not (F(x)=\Pi_x(H)).
+
+We apply Nishioka's special-value theorem
+\cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues} to the reduced form
+of
+\[
+ P_0(z)F(z^2)-P_1(z)F(z)^2=0.
+\]
+In her notation one may take (p=2), (N=0), (n=1), (m=2),
+(M=2), (U=1), and coefficient-growth exponent (L=1).  The required
+numerical inequality is (M(p+N)n^2=4<2^{2+1/L}=8).  The integer
+coefficients and analyticity of (F) give the required linear coefficient
+height bound, while the strict gaps ensure that the reduced coefficient
+polynomials do not vanish anywhere on the orbit (x,x^2,x^4,\ldots).
+Consequently, if (F) were transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then (F(x))
+would be transcendental.
+
+Assume (i).  Positivity and \eqref{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
+give (F(x)=1), so the cited theorem forces (F) to be algebraic.  By
+\Cref{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}, (H=\delta R) for the unique
+normalized rational (R).  Now
+\Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} gives
+(1=\Pi_x(H)=R(x)^{-2}) and (R(x)>0), hence (R(x)=1).  This proves (ii).
+Conversely, (ii) and \eqref{eq:rational-mahler-telescope} give (i), and the
+same proposition gives uniqueness.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{remark}[Scope of the lifting theorem]
+The determinant parity in \Cref{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting} is essential
+to the integrality step, so the theorem does not assert the converse for an
+arbitrary positive rational (H).  Its realizable class is nevertheless broad.
+Fix (r\ge2), an odd (a>0), and a positive even (b), and let (A) have
+diagonal entries (a) and off-diagonal entries (b).  Then
+\(\lambda=a+(r-1)b\).  Any diagonal (B=\operatorname{diag}(c_i)) and
+(B'=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)), with odd
+\(\abs{c_i},\abs{d_i}\le a\), satisfies the same-base compatibility and
+strict gaps, and realizes
+\[
+ H(z)=\frac{\prod_i(1-c_i z)}{\prod_i(1-d_i z)}.
+\]
 \end{remark}

+def critical_mahler_normalization_matches() -> bool:
+    """Verify that the weighted product is F(x)^2, rather than F(x)."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    x = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+    h = (1 - z) / (1 + z)
+    f = 1 - z
+    symbolic = all(
+        (
+            sp.cancel(f**2 - h * f.subs(z, z**2)) == 0,
+            f.subs(z, x) == sp.Rational(2, 3),
+            f.subs(z, x) ** 2 == sp.Rational(4, 9),
+            f.subs(z, x) != f.subs(z, x) ** 2,
+        )
+    )
+    if not symbolic:
+        return False
+
+    with mp.workdps(80):
+        real_x = mp.mpf(1) / 3
+        logarithmic_product = mp.fsum(
+            mp.power(2, -nu)
+            * mp.log((1 - real_x ** (2**nu)) / (1 + real_x ** (2**nu)))
+            for nu in range(12)
+        )
+        product_value = mp.exp(logarithmic_product)
+        return (
+            abs(product_value - mp.mpf(4) / 9) < mp.mpf("1e-70")
+            and abs(product_value - (1 - real_x)) > mp.mpf("1e-2")
+        )
+
+
+def _critical_mahler_coefficients(order: int) -> tuple[sp.Integer, ...]:
+    """Solve F^2=((1-z)/(1-3z))F(z^2) coefficient by coefficient."""
+    h_coefficients = [sp.Integer(1)] + [
+        2 * sp.Integer(3) ** (degree - 1) for degree in range(1, order + 1)
+    ]
+    coefficients = [sp.Integer(1)]
+    for degree in range(1, order + 1):
+        known_square = sum(
+            coefficients[index] * coefficients[degree - index]
+            for index in range(1, degree)
+        )
+        right_hand_side = sum(
+            h_coefficients[degree - 2 * index] * coefficients[index]
+            for index in range(degree // 2 + 1)
+        )
+        coefficients.append(sp.simplify((right_hand_side - known_square) / 2))
+    return tuple(coefficients)
+
+
+def critical_mahler_integrality_matches(order: int = 24) -> bool:
+    """Check determinant parity, integral recursion, and the truncated equation."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    p_zero = 1 - z
+    p_one = 1 - 3 * z
+    coefficients = _critical_mahler_coefficients(order)
+    f = sum(coefficient * z**degree for degree, coefficient in enumerate(coefficients))
+    residual = sp.series(
+        f**2 - (p_zero / p_one) * f.subs(z, z**2), z, 0, order + 1
+    ).removeO()
+    return all(
+        (
+            sp.Poly(p_zero - p_one, z).all_coeffs()[-1] % 2 == 0,
+            all(coefficient.is_Integer for coefficient in coefficients),
+            sp.expand(residual) == 0,
+        )
+    )
+
+
+def critical_zero_estimate_pullback_matches() -> bool:
+    """Check the cleared pullback identity and its two bidegree bounds."""
+    z, y = sp.symbols("z y")
+    p_zero = 1 - z
+    p_one = 1 - 3 * z
+    q = y**2 + z * y + z + 1
+    d = sp.Poly(q, z, y).degree(z)
+    n = sp.Poly(q, z, y).degree(y)
+    eta = max(sp.degree(p_zero, z), sp.degree(p_one, z))
+    pullback = sp.cancel(
+        p_zero**n * q.subs({z: z**2, y: p_one * y**2 / p_zero}, simultaneous=True)
+    )
+    pullback = sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).as_expr()
+    coefficients = _critical_mahler_coefficients(18)
+    f = sum(coefficient * z**degree for degree, coefficient in enumerate(coefficients))
+    evaluated_pullback = sp.series(pullback.subs(y, f), z, 0, 19).removeO()
+    expected = sp.series(
+        p_zero**n * q.subs({z: z**2, y: f.subs(z, z**2)}, simultaneous=True),
+        z,
+        0,
+        19,
+    ).removeO()
+    return all(
+        (
+            sp.Poly(q, z, y).is_irreducible,
+            sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).degree(y) <= 2 * n,
+            sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).degree(z) <= 2 * d + eta * n,
+            sp.expand(evaluated_pullback - expected) == 0,
+        )
+    )
+
+
+def rational_mahler_saturation_matches() -> bool:
+    """Verify normalized saturation identities in exact rational examples."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    examples = (
+        ((1 - z) ** 2 * (1 + 2 * z) / ((1 - 3 * z) * (1 + z) ** 3), 2),
+        ((1 + z + z**2) / ((1 - 2 * z) ** 2 * (1 + 3 * z)), 3),
+        ((1 - 4 * z) * (1 + z) ** 2 / (1 + 2 * z**2), 5),
+    )
+    for rational_r, exponent in examples:
+        rational_r = sp.cancel(rational_r)
+        h = sp.cancel(rational_r.subs(z, z**2) / rational_r**2)
+        q = sp.cancel(rational_r**exponent)
+        delta_q = sp.cancel(q.subs(z, z**2) / q**2)
+        numerator, denominator = sp.fraction(q)
+        factor_exponents = [
+            multiplicity
+            for polynomial in (numerator, denominator)
+            for _factor, multiplicity in sp.factor_list(polynomial)[1]
+        ]
+        if not all(
+            (
+                rational_r.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                h.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                q.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                sp.cancel(h**exponent - delta_q) == 0,
+                all(multiplicity % exponent == 0 for multiplicity in factor_exponents),
+            )
+        ):
+            return False
+    return True

+\begin{lemma}[Critical quadratic zero estimate]

+\begin{lemma}[Normalized saturation of rational coboundaries]
+\label{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}
+Let \(H,Q\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=Q(0)=1\).  If, for some
+integer \(m\ge1\),
+\[
+ H^m=\delta Q=\frac{Q(z^2)}{Q(z)^2},
+\]
+then there is an \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), with \(R(0)=1\), such that
+\(H=\delta R\).
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+For \(a\in\overline{\QQ}^\times\), let \(h(a)\) and \(q(a)\) denote the
+coefficients of \([a]\) in the divisors of \(H\) and \(Q\), respectively.
+Taking divisors gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:saturation-divisor-recurrence}
+ mh(a)=q(a^2)-2q(a),
+ \qquad q(a^2)\equiv2q(a)\pmod m.
+\end{equation}
+Fix \(a\ne0,\infty\).  For sufficiently large \(N\), among the
+\(2^N\)-th roots of \(a\) choose \(b_N\) outside the finite support of
+\(\operatorname{div}Q\).  Iterating the congruence along the chain from
+\(b_N\) to \(a\) gives \(q(a)\equiv2^Nq(b_N)\equiv0\pmod m\).
+The coefficient at zero is zero because \(Q(0)=1\), and the degree-zero
+condition on a principal divisor gives the same divisibility at infinity.
+Thus \(\operatorname{div}Q=mD\).
+
+The divisor \(D\) is Galois invariant and has degree zero.  Since
+\(\operatorname{Pic}^0(\mathbb P^1_{\QQ})=0\), choose
+\(S\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(\operatorname{div}S=D\), normalized by
+\(S(0)=1\).  Then \(Q/S^m\) is constant, and evaluation at zero gives
+\(Q=S^m\).  It follows that \((H/\delta S)^m=1\).  This rational function is
+constant and has value one at zero, so \(H=\delta S\); take \(R=S\).
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{proposition}[Algebraic critical products are rational coboundaries]
+\label{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}
+Let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\), \(H(0)=1\), and suppose that
+\(F\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) is algebraic over \(\CC(z)\) and satisfies
+\(F(z)^2=H(z)F(z^2)\).  Then \(H=\delta R\) for a unique
+\(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(R(0)=1\).
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(G=zF'/F\).  Logarithmic differentiation gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:log-derivative-mahler}
+ G(z)=G(z^2)+\frac z2\frac{H'(z)}{H(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+If the rational inhomogeneous term is non-zero, the equations at \(z\) and
+\(z^2\) eliminate it to give a homogeneous scalar (2)-Mahler equation for
+\(G\); if it is zero, \eqref{eq:log-derivative-mahler} and \(G(0)=0\) give
+\(G=0\).  Since algebraic functions are D-finite, B\'ezivin's theorem that a
+D-finite Mahler function is rational
+\cite[Theorem~1]{BellCoonsRowland2013MahlerDichotomy} yields
+\(G\in\CC(z)\), and its rational Taylor coefficients give
+\(G\in\QQ(z)\).
+
+All analytic branches of the algebraic function \(F\) have the same rational
+logarithmic derivative, so their pairwise quotients are constants.  Finite
+monodromy therefore gives an \(m\ge1\) for which
+\(T=F^m\) is single-valued, hence \(T\in\CC(z)^\times\).  Its Taylor
+coefficients give \(T\in\QQ(z)^\times\), and \(T(0)=1\).  Raising the
+functional equation to the (m)-th power gives
+\[
+ H^m=\frac{T(z)^2}{T(z^2)}=\delta(T^{-1}).
+\]
+Apply \Cref{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}, and then use the normalized
+injectivity proved in \Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} for uniqueness.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{theorem}[Strict-gap determinant boundary lifting]
+\label{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting}
+Let \(A\) be a primitive non-negative integer matrix with Perron root
+\(\lambda>1\), and put \(x=\lambda^{-1}\).  Let \(B,B'\) be integer matrices
+of the same size such that, entrywise,
+\[
+ \abs{B_{ij}},\abs{B'_{ij}}\le A_{ij},
+ \qquad B_{ij}\equiv B'_{ij}\equiv A_{ij}\pmod2,
+\]
+and suppose that \(\rad(B),\rad(B')<\lambda\).  Set
+\[
+ H(z)=\frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}.
+\]
+Then the following are equivalent:
+\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
+ \item \(\Pi_x(H)=1\);
+ \item there is a unique \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) such that
+ \[
+  R(0)=R(x)=1,
+  \qquad H(z)=\frac{R(z^2)}{R(z)^2}.
+ \]
+\end{enumerate}
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The strict gaps imply that both determinant polynomials are non-zero on a disk
+\(\abs z<r\) for some \(x<r<1\).  They are positive on \([0,x]\), because
+they are real, non-zero there, and equal one at zero.  Hence (H>0) on that
+interval.  Define (F) by \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-product}.  By
+\Cref{lem:critical-mahler-integrality}, it is analytic on \(\abs z<r\), has
+integer coefficients, and satisfies \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-equation}.
+Crucially, the product normalization is
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
+ F(x)^2=\Pi_x(H),
+\end{equation}
+not (F(x)=\Pi_x(H)).
+
+We apply Nishioka's special-value theorem
+\cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues} to the reduced form
+of
+\[
+ P_0(z)F(z^2)-P_1(z)F(z)^2=0.
+\]
+In her notation one may take (p=2), (N=0), (n=1), (m=2),
+(M=2), (U=1), and coefficient-growth exponent (L=1).  The required
+numerical inequality is (M(p+N)n^2=4<2^{2+1/L}=8).  The integer
+coefficients and analyticity of (F) give the required linear coefficient
+height bound, while the strict gaps ensure that the reduced coefficient
+polynomials do not vanish anywhere on the orbit (x,x^2,x^4,\ldots).
+Consequently, if (F) were transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then (F(x))
+would be transcendental.
+
+Assume (i).  Positivity and \eqref{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
+give (F(x)=1), so the cited theorem forces (F) to be algebraic.  By
+\Cref{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}, (H=\delta R) for the unique
+normalized rational (R).  Now
+\Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} gives
+(1=\Pi_x(H)=R(x)^{-2}) and (R(x)>0), hence (R(x)=1).  This proves (ii).
+Conversely, (ii) and \eqref{eq:rational-mahler-telescope} give (i), and the
+same proposition gives uniqueness.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{remark}[Scope of the lifting theorem]
+The determinant parity in \Cref{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting} is essential
+to the integrality step, so the theorem does not assert the converse for an
+arbitrary positive rational (H).  Its realizable class is nevertheless broad.
+Fix (r\ge2), an odd (a>0), and a positive even (b), and let (A) have
+diagonal entries (a) and off-diagonal entries (b).  Then
+\(\lambda=a+(r-1)b\).  Any diagonal (B=\operatorname{diag}(c_i)) and
+(B'=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)), with odd
+\(\abs{c_i},\abs{d_i}\le a\), satisfies the same-base compatibility and
+strict gaps, and realizes
+\[
+ H(z)=\frac{\prod_i(1-c_i z)}{\prod_i(1-d_i z)}.
+\]
 \end{remark}

+def critical_mahler_normalization_matches() -> bool:
+    """Verify that the weighted product is F(x)^2, rather than F(x)."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    x = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+    h = (1 - z) / (1 + z)
+    f = 1 - z
+    symbolic = all(
+        (
+            sp.cancel(f**2 - h * f.subs(z, z**2)) == 0,
+            f.subs(z, x) == sp.Rational(2, 3),
+            f.subs(z, x) ** 2 == sp.Rational(4, 9),
+            f.subs(z, x) != f.subs(z, x) ** 2,
+        )
+    )
+    if not symbolic:
+        return False
+
+    with mp.workdps(80):
+        real_x = mp.mpf(1) / 3
+        logarithmic_product = mp.fsum(
+            mp.power(2, -nu)
+            * mp.log((1 - real_x ** (2**nu)) / (1 + real_x ** (2**nu)))
+            for nu in range(12)
+        )
+        product_value = mp.exp(logarithmic_product)
+        return (
+            abs(product_value - mp.mpf(4) / 9) < mp.mpf("1e-70")
+            and abs(product_value - (1 - real_x)) > mp.mpf("1e-2")
+        )
+
+
+def _critical_mahler_coefficients(order: int) -> tuple[sp.Integer, ...]:
+    """Solve F^2=((1-z)/(1-3z))F(z^2) coefficient by coefficient."""
+    h_coefficients = [sp.Integer(1)] + [
+        2 * sp.Integer(3) ** (degree - 1) for degree in range(1, order + 1)
+    ]
+    coefficients = [sp.Integer(1)]
+    for degree in range(1, order + 1):
+        known_square = sum(
+            coefficients[index] * coefficients[degree - index]
+            for index in range(1, degree)
+        )
+        right_hand_side = sum(
+            h_coefficients[degree - 2 * index] * coefficients[index]
+            for index in range(degree // 2 + 1)
+        )
+        coefficients.append(sp.simplify((right_hand_side - known_square) / 2))
+    return tuple(coefficients)
+
+
+def critical_mahler_integrality_matches(order: int = 24) -> bool:
+    """Check determinant parity, integral recursion, and the truncated equation."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    p_zero = 1 - z
+    p_one = 1 - 3 * z
+    coefficients = _critical_mahler_coefficients(order)
+    f = sum(coefficient * z**degree for degree, coefficient in enumerate(coefficients))
+    residual = sp.series(
+        f**2 - (p_zero / p_one) * f.subs(z, z**2), z, 0, order + 1
+    ).removeO()
+    return all(
+        (
+            sp.Poly(p_zero - p_one, z).all_coeffs()[-1] % 2 == 0,
+            all(coefficient.is_Integer for coefficient in coefficients),
+            sp.expand(residual) == 0,
+        )
+    )
+
+
+def critical_zero_estimate_pullback_matches() -> bool:
+    """Check the cleared pullback identity and its two bidegree bounds."""
+    z, y = sp.symbols("z y")
+    p_zero = 1 - z
+    p_one = 1 - 3 * z
+    q = y**2 + z * y + z + 1
+    d = sp.Poly(q, z, y).degree(z)
+    n = sp.Poly(q, z, y).degree(y)
+    eta = max(sp.degree(p_zero, z), sp.degree(p_one, z))
+    pullback = sp.cancel(
+        p_zero**n * q.subs({z: z**2, y: p_one * y**2 / p_zero}, simultaneous=True)
+    )
+    pullback = sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).as_expr()
+    coefficients = _critical_mahler_coefficients(18)
+    f = sum(coefficient * z**degree for degree, coefficient in enumerate(coefficients))
+    evaluated_pullback = sp.series(pullback.subs(y, f), z, 0, 19).removeO()
+    expected = sp.series(
+        p_zero**n * q.subs({z: z**2, y: f.subs(z, z**2)}, simultaneous=True),
+        z,
+        0,
+        19,
+    ).removeO()
+    return all(
+        (
+            sp.Poly(q, z, y).is_irreducible,
+            sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).degree(y) <= 2 * n,
+            sp.Poly(pullback, z, y).degree(z) <= 2 * d + eta * n,
+            sp.expand(evaluated_pullback - expected) == 0,
+        )
+    )
+
+
+def rational_mahler_saturation_matches() -> bool:
+    """Verify normalized saturation identities in exact rational examples."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    examples = (
+        ((1 - z) ** 2 * (1 + 2 * z) / ((1 - 3 * z) * (1 + z) ** 3), 2),
+        ((1 + z + z**2) / ((1 - 2 * z) ** 2 * (1 + 3 * z)), 3),
+        ((1 - 4 * z) * (1 + z) ** 2 / (1 + 2 * z**2), 5),
+    )
+    for rational_r, exponent in examples:
+        rational_r = sp.cancel(rational_r)
+        h = sp.cancel(rational_r.subs(z, z**2) / rational_r**2)
+        q = sp.cancel(rational_r**exponent)
+        delta_q = sp.cancel(q.subs(z, z**2) / q**2)
+        numerator, denominator = sp.fraction(q)
+        factor_exponents = [
+            multiplicity
+            for polynomial in (numerator, denominator)
+            for _factor, multiplicity in sp.factor_list(polynomial)[1]
+        ]
+        if not all(
+            (
+                rational_r.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                h.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                q.subs(z, 0) == 1,
+                sp.cancel(h**exponent - delta_q) == 0,
+                all(multiplicity % exponent == 0 for multiplicity in factor_exponents),
+            )
+        ):
+            return False
+    return True
+

+\eqref{eq:critical-mahler-product}.  For an odd prime \(p\), compare the
+coefficient of \(z^n\) in \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-equation}.  Its left-hand
+side is \(2f_n\) plus an expression in \(f_0,\ldots,f_{n-1}\), while its
+right-hand side belongs to \(\ZZ_p\) whenever the preceding coefficients do,
+because \(P_1(0)=1\).  Induction and \(2\in\ZZ_p^\times\) give
+\(F\in\ZZ_p[[z]]\) for every odd \(p\).  A rational number integral at every
+prime is an integer, proving the claim coefficientwise.
+\end{proof}
+
+The next estimate is not needed to reprove the special-value theorem below;
+it records an effective feature of the critical quadratic equation itself.
+
+\begin{lemma}[Critical quadratic zero estimate]
+\label{lem:critical-mahler-zero-estimate}
+Let \(P_0,P_1\in\CC[z]\) have constant term one, set
+\(\eta=\max\{\deg P_0,\deg P_1\}\), and let an analytic germ
+\(F(0)=1\) satisfy
+\[
+ P_1(z)F(z)^2=P_0(z)F(z^2).
+\]
+If \(F\) is transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then every non-zero
+\(Q\in\CC[z,Y]\) with \(\deg_zQ\le D\) and \(\deg_YQ\le N\) satisfies
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-mahler-zero-bound}
+ \operatorname{ord}_{z=0}Q(z,F(z))
+ \le D+4DN+\eta N^2.
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+First take an irreducible factor \(q\in\CC[z,Y]\) of positive
+\(Y\)-degree and write \(d=\deg_zq\), \(n=\deg_Yq\).  Clear the denominator
+in its pullback by setting
+\[
+ \widetilde q(z,Y)=P_0(z)^n
+ q\!\left(z^2,\frac{P_1(z)}{P_0(z)}Y^2\right).
+\]
+This is a polynomial, with
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-pullback-orders}
+ \deg_Y\widetilde q=2n,\qquad
+ \deg_z\widetilde q\le2d+\eta n,\qquad
+ \operatorname{ord}_0\widetilde q(z,F(z))
+ =2\operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z)).
+\end{equation}
+We claim that \(q\nmid\widetilde q\).  Otherwise the irreducible curve
+\(C:q=0\) is invariant under the rational map
+\[
+ \Phi(z,Y)=\left(z^2,\frac{P_1(z)}{P_0(z)}Y^2\right).
+\]
+Pass to the normalization of \(C\).  The induced map permutes forward the
+finite set of places above \((0,1)\), so this finite dynamical system contains
+a periodic place.  Its Puiseux germ \(Y=G(z)\), based at \((0,1)\), therefore
+satisfies for some \(\ell\ge1\) the \(\ell\)-fold iterate of the same equation
+as \(F\).  Consequently \(U=G/F\) obeys
+\[
+ U(z^{2^\ell})=U(z)^{2^\ell},\qquad U(0)=1.
+\]
+If \(U=1+cz^\alpha+\cdots\), with \(c\ne0\) and the least positive Puiseux
+exponent \(\alpha\), the least non-constant exponents on the two sides are
+respectively \(2^\ell\alpha\) and \(\alpha\), a contradiction.  Thus
+\(U=1\), which would make \(F=G\) algebraic.  This proves the claim.
+
+Hence \(R_q(z)=\operatorname{Res}_Y(q,\widetilde q)\) is non-zero.  A
+B\'ezout identity in \(Y\), evaluated at \(Y=F(z)\), and
+\eqref{eq:critical-pullback-orders} imply
 \[
- \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
- =\frac{\prod_i(1-c_i z)}{\prod_i(1-d_i z)}.
+ \operatorname{ord}_0q(z,F(z))
+ \le\operatorname{ord}_0R_q
+ \le\deg R_q
+ \le4dn+\eta n^2.
 \]
-Thus the omitted converse already contains multiplicative-relation questions
-for weighted products built from these linear factors; it is not an artifact
-of dropping the same-base compatibility or strict-gap hypotheses.
+Finally write \(Q=a(z)\prod_iq_i^{e_i}\), separating its polynomial content
+in \(z\).  The content contributes at most \(D\).  With multiplicities,
+\(\sum_i e_id_i\le D\) and \(\sum_i e_in_i\le N\); therefore
+\(\sum_i e_id_in_i\le DN\) and
+\(\sum_i e_in_i^2\le N^2\).  Summing the factor bounds proves
+\eqref{eq:critical-mahler-zero-bound}.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Normalized saturation of rational coboundaries]
+\label{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}
+Let \(H,Q\in\QQ(z)^\times\) satisfy \(H(0)=Q(0)=1\).  If, for some
+integer \(m\ge1\),
+\[
+ H^m=\delta Q=\frac{Q(z^2)}{Q(z)^2},
+\]
+then there is an \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\), with \(R(0)=1\), such that
+\(H=\delta R\).
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+For \(a\in\overline{\QQ}^\times\), let \(h(a)\) and \(q(a)\) denote the
+coefficients of \([a]\) in the divisors of \(H\) and \(Q\), respectively.
+Taking divisors gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:saturation-divisor-recurrence}
+ mh(a)=q(a^2)-2q(a),
+ \qquad q(a^2)\equiv2q(a)\pmod m.
+\end{equation}
+Fix \(a\ne0,\infty\).  For sufficiently large \(N\), among the
+\(2^N\)-th roots of \(a\) choose \(b_N\) outside the finite support of
+\(\operatorname{div}Q\).  Iterating the congruence along the chain from
+\(b_N\) to \(a\) gives \(q(a)\equiv2^Nq(b_N)\equiv0\pmod m\).
+The coefficient at zero is zero because \(Q(0)=1\), and the degree-zero
+condition on a principal divisor gives the same divisibility at infinity.
+Thus \(\operatorname{div}Q=mD\).
+
+The divisor \(D\) is Galois invariant and has degree zero.  Since
+\(\operatorname{Pic}^0(\mathbb P^1_{\QQ})=0\), choose
+\(S\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(\operatorname{div}S=D\), normalized by
+\(S(0)=1\).  Then \(Q/S^m\) is constant, and evaluation at zero gives
+\(Q=S^m\).  It follows that \((H/\delta S)^m=1\).  This rational function is
+constant and has value one at zero, so \(H=\delta S\); take \(R=S\).
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{proposition}[Algebraic critical products are rational coboundaries]
+\label{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}
+Let \(H\in\QQ(z)^\times\), \(H(0)=1\), and suppose that
+\(F\in1+z\QQ[[z]]\) is algebraic over \(\CC(z)\) and satisfies
+\(F(z)^2=H(z)F(z^2)\).  Then \(H=\delta R\) for a unique
+\(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) with \(R(0)=1\).
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Put \(G=zF'/F\).  Logarithmic differentiation gives
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:log-derivative-mahler}
+ G(z)=G(z^2)+\frac z2\frac{H'(z)}{H(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+If the rational inhomogeneous term is non-zero, the equations at \(z\) and
+\(z^2\) eliminate it to give a homogeneous scalar \(2\)-Mahler equation for
+\(G\); if it is zero, \eqref{eq:log-derivative-mahler} and \(G(0)=0\) give
+\(G=0\).  Since algebraic functions are D-finite, B\'ezivin's theorem that a
+D-finite Mahler function is rational
+\cite[Theorem~1]{BellCoonsRowland2013MahlerDichotomy} yields
+\(G\in\CC(z)\), and its rational Taylor coefficients give
+\(G\in\QQ(z)\).
+
+All analytic branches of the algebraic function \(F\) have the same rational
+logarithmic derivative, so their pairwise quotients are constants.  Finite
+monodromy therefore gives an \(m\ge1\) for which
+\(T=F^m\) is single-valued, hence \(T\in\CC(z)^\times\).  Its Taylor
+coefficients give \(T\in\QQ(z)^\times\), and \(T(0)=1\).  Raising the
+functional equation to the \(m\)-th power gives
+\[
+ H^m=\frac{T(z)^2}{T(z^2)}=\delta(T^{-1}).
+\]
+Apply \Cref{lem:rational-mahler-saturation}, and then use the normalized
+injectivity proved in \Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} for uniqueness.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{theorem}[Strict-gap determinant boundary lifting]
+\label{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting}
+Let \(A\) be a primitive non-negative integer matrix with Perron root
+\(\lambda>1\), and put \(x=\lambda^{-1}\).  Let \(B,B'\) be integer matrices
+of the same size such that, entrywise,
+\[
+ \abs{B_{ij}},\abs{B'_{ij}}\le A_{ij},
+ \qquad B_{ij}\equiv B'_{ij}\equiv A_{ij}\pmod2,
+\]
+and suppose that \(\rad(B),\rad(B')<\lambda\).  Set
+\[
+ H(z)=\frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}.
+\]
+Then the following are equivalent:
+\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
+ \item \(\Pi_x(H)=1\);
+ \item there is a unique \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) such that
+ \[
+  R(0)=R(x)=1,
+  \qquad H(z)=\frac{R(z^2)}{R(z)^2}.
+ \]
+\end{enumerate}
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The strict gaps imply that both determinant polynomials are non-zero on a disk
+\(\abs z<r\) for some \(x<r<1\).  They are positive on \([0,x]\), because
+they are real, non-zero there, and equal one at zero.  Hence (H>0) on that
+interval.  Define (F) by \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-product}.  By
+\Cref{lem:critical-mahler-integrality}, it is analytic on \(\abs z<r\), has
+integer coefficients, and satisfies \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-equation}.
+Crucially, the product normalization is
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
+ F(x)^2=\Pi_x(H),
+\end{equation}
+not (F(x)=\Pi_x(H)).
+
+We apply Nishioka's special-value theorem
+\cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues} to the reduced form
+of
+\[
+ P_0(z)F(z^2)-P_1(z)F(z)^2=0.
+\]
+In her notation one may take (p=2), (N=0), (n=1), (m=2),
+(M=2), (U=1), and coefficient-growth exponent (L=1).  The required
+numerical inequality is (M(p+N)n^2=4<2^{2+1/L}=8).  The integer
+coefficients and analyticity of (F) give the required linear coefficient
+height bound, while the strict gaps ensure that the reduced coefficient
+polynomials do not vanish anywhere on the orbit (x,x^2,x^4,\ldots).
+Consequently, if (F) were transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then (F(x))
+would be transcendental.
+
+Assume (i).  Positivity and \eqref{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
+give (F(x)=1), so the cited theorem forces (F) to be algebraic.  By
+\Cref{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}, (H=\delta R) for the unique
+normalized rational (R).  Now
+\Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} gives
+(1=\Pi_x(H)=R(x)^{-2}) and (R(x)>0), hence (R(x)=1).  This proves (ii).
+Conversely, (ii) and \eqref{eq:rational-mahler-telescope} give (i), and the
+same proposition gives uniqueness.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{remark}[Scope of the lifting theorem]
+The determinant parity in \Cref{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting} is essential
+to the integrality step, so the theorem does not assert the converse for an
+arbitrary positive rational (H).  Its realizable class is nevertheless broad.
+Fix (r\ge2), an odd (a>0), and a positive even (b), and let (A) have
+diagonal entries (a) and off-diagonal entries (b).  Then
+\(\lambda=a+(r-1)b\).  Any diagonal (B=\operatorname{diag}(c_i)) and
+(B'=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)), with odd
+\(\abs{c_i},\abs{d_i}\le a\), satisfies the same-base compatibility and
+strict gaps, and realizes
+\[
+ H(z)=\frac{\prod_i(1-c_i z)}{\prod_i(1-d_i z)}.
+\]
 \end{remark}
 
 This mechanism is strictly weaker than full \(G\)-cospectrality, equivalently
